blocks.title: Linear regression
blocks.text: Linear regression models the relationship between two variables to predict one from the other: Y = b0 + b1 X + error, where Y is the dependent variable, X the independent variable, b0 the intercept (Y when X = 0), b1 the slope (change in Y per unit of X) and the error term the gap between predicted and actual values.

blocks.caption: Fruit stall: customers and daily earnings

blocks.text: Every 5 extra customers add 200 rupees, so the slope b1 = 200 / 5 = 40 rupees per customer. Using 10 customers and 500 rupees: 500 = b0 + 40 x 10, so b0 = 100, the base earnings with no customers. The model is earnings = 100 + 40 x customers. For 22 customers it predicts 100 + 880 = 980 rupees. On day 6, 28 customers gave 1,250 rupees while the model predicted 100 + 1,120 = 1,220; the error is 30 rupees (actual minus predicted), showing real data vary.

blocks.alt: Top left: five points of customers against earnings on the line earnings = 100 + 40 x customers, with a prediction of Rs 980 for 22 customers and an actual day-6 point of 1,250. Top right: an S-shaped probability curve over pass/fail points for 1 to 6 hours of study. Bottom left: Math and English scores of five students in two K-means clusters with centres marked x. Bottom right: five model-building steps.
blocks.caption: Linear regression, logistic regression and K-means (original diagram after topic 5.4).
blocks.long_description: The fruit-stall data lie exactly on the line earnings = 100 + 40 x customers, so 22 customers predict 980 rupees, and on day 6 the model predicted 1,220 for 28 customers against an actual 1,250. A logistic model turns study hours into a probability of passing that rises in an S-shape from near 0 to near 1, crossing 0.5 between the failing and passing students; the curve drawn is illustrative. K-means with K = 2 groups Basim, Umer and Maliha around a centre at Math 78.3, English 65, and Anie and Tallat around Math 45, English 82.5. A model is built by defining the problem, collecting data, choosing an algorithm, training and evaluating on new data.

blocks.prompt: Which is a basic statistical model (MCQ 1)? What does the slope represent (MCQ 5)? Name one basic model for predicting outcomes and explain its purpose (short question 2).
blocks.explanation: (a) linear regression; (b) the change in the dependent variable for a unit change in the independent variable. Linear regression predicts a numeric outcome from another variable by fitting a straight line, for example a stall's earnings from its number of customers.

items: Linear regression: earnings = 100 + 40 x customers; 22 customers give Rs 980; the day-6 error is Rs 30.
